channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] CISA puts a number on the water campaign — more than 100 internet-exposed systems targeted in July
item.description: Publishing exposure-reduction guidance on 26 August, CISA said for the first time how large July’s water-sector wave actually was: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. At least a dozen states were touched, and CISA records no significant disruption to water service. The government links the activity to Iranian actors and says it was aimed at operational technology rather than data. What makes this the week’s most useful item for OT defenders is not the number but the admission behind it: the exposure that enabled it was never in anybody’s asset register. The guidance is written for every sector — identify what is internet-accessible using external scanning as well as internal inventories, then remove what operations do not require. - CISA Exposure Reduction guidance — corroborated by SecurityWeek, TechCrunch and The Register - Guidance published and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Boston Scientific says a cyberattack is causing a global disruption — orders and shipments are the casualty
item.description: One of the world’s largest medical device manufacturers confirmed on 26 August, in a statement and an SEC filing, that an attack detected the previous day is disrupting operations worldwide — specifically a network outage affecting access to certain operating systems and business applications, including its ability to process and ship customer orders. Boston Scientific runs 13 manufacturing sites, employs roughly 59,000 people and sells into 127 countries, so the blast radius reaches hospitals waiting on pacemakers, defibrillators and catheters. The company has activated incident response and engaged outside investigators, but has not named an attacker or entry route, said whether data was taken, or given a restoration date. Nothing has been confirmed about plant-floor control systems. That distinction is the lesson rather than a reassurance: order management, warehouse and shipping systems sit outside most OT programmes, yet losing them stops product moving just as effectively as stopping a line. - Boston Scientific statement and SEC filing — reported by BleepingComputer, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch, The Register and CBS News - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through internet-wide scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named — including F-series safety controllers — across critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance and capability development positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk. They also flag a blind spot worth acting on: where a system integrator or MSP holds remote access, the asset owner frequently does not know the controller is internet-reachable at all. The related campaign against water-sector controllers is where the confirmed damage sits — attackers modified or deleted project-file logic, manipulated HMI and SCADA display data, and disabled shutdown and alarm functions, creating unsafe conditions with no operator notification. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A and the FBI water-sector alert — via CISA, BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026 (advisory PDF posted 18 Aug), re-verified 26 Aug 2026 12:35 PM ET; FBI water-sector alert 4 Aug 2026; campaign ongoing since 27 Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and is rewriting the sector’s cyber rules
item.description: A small UK gas-fired generating site was taken offline for four days, in what officials describe as the first successful cyberattack of its kind on British energy infrastructure. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero confirms a cyberattack impacted a small-scale energy generator, stresses the national grid and customer supply were never at risk, and — the part defenders should note — says sector cybersecurity regulations are now being updated. The four-day duration and the Iran attribution remain press-sourced, carried by the Telegraph and picked up widely; the NCSC has not commented and the facility has not been named. The affected site sat below the threshold at which generators must report cyber incidents. That exposed population is embedded generation, CHP and district energy, standby and peaking plant, battery storage and small renewables — unmanned assets reached through vendor remote access or a cellular router, sitting under the regulatory floor. The disclosure landed the same week the US Treasury sanctioned Iranian nationals over intrusions at energy companies, which is why the two stories are being read together even though neither government has joined them. - On-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, reported via SecurityWeek, The Record and Help Net Security; duration and attribution from the Sunday Telegraph - Telegraph report published 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement 23 Aug 2026; trade-press pickup 24 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026 with no new technical detail released; attack occurred July 2026, exact date not published

item.title: [Critical] US seizes the Chinese state-sponsored scanning and relay network built out of other people’s IoT devices
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 26 August that they had seized the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms operated by a PRC state-sponsored group DOJ tracks as QTFY and ties to a Nanjing technology company. QScan automatically scans for and infects internet-facing IoT devices worldwide; QTRouter then enrols those devices, alongside commercial proxy services and leased virtual private servers, into a network that hides the Chinese origin of intrusions. DOJ says the service was sold on to customers including China’s Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army. Named victims include NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy, HHS and the US Senate, with power companies, hospitals, telecoms and defence contractors among private targets. Because the seized domains were hard-coded into both malware families, the takedown rendered them inoperable. For OT operators the uncomfortable part is the raw material rather than the target list: the cameras, cellular gateways and routers sitting unmanaged at remote sites are exactly what this infrastructure is built from. - US Department of Justice press release and court documents — corroborated by CNBC and ITPro - Announced 26 Aug 2026; verified against the DOJ release the same day

item.title: [Critical] Washington sanctions an Iranian cyber network inside US critical infrastructure — but not the crew touching the controllers
item.description: Treasury designated a Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, and the detail matters more than the headline: the network named is an espionage and theft cluster, not the one manipulating process equipment. Treasury says its members — five of them indicted by the Justice Department the week before — have been breaching and exfiltrating data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. That is access collection, and the same footholds convert to disruption when tasking changes. Running alongside it, still formally unattributed by CISA, is the campaign that has degraded water operations across at least a dozen states through internet-facing controllers. The State Department has posted a reward notice on the wider problem. Two clusters, one adversary, one of them named — and the naming changes your legal position long before it changes your exposure. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; State Department Rewards for Justice notice; reported via The Record, Nextgov/FCW and The Hacker News - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026 — no further designations or CISA attribution issued

item.title: [High] CISA ran the same attack against a water utility and a government body — one caught it, the other never noticed
item.description: Advisory AA26-237A, published on 25 August, reports two simultaneous CISA red-team assessments run with comparable tradecraft against two critical-infrastructure organisations. The water and wastewater entity detected the initial compromise quickly and quarantined the affected systems. The government services organisation did not: the team landed on four workstations after finding a web application still using default credentials for built-in accounts, phished from an internal address, took domain privileges, and moved into sensitive business systems and cloud resources without triggering a response — eventually reading the security team’s own email and putting keyloggers on defenders’ machines. CISA’s explanation is the part worth circulating internally. Thousands of false positives from routine business activity, many rated high, buried the real alerts. Multiple SOCs and endpoint tools ran with no shared visibility. Analysts had neither escalation procedures nor authority to act. A genuine alert on a configuration-management server was closed as a false positive because nobody could work out who owned the box. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 4,407 controllers are answering from the public internet — and 22 of them sit in the towns being attacked
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs scanned for controllers responding on EtherNet/IP port 44818 and found 4,407 exposed worldwide on 3 August, 2,844 of them in the United States, with Canada and Spain next. Twenty-two of those hosts were in cities named in the ongoing water-utility campaign, and 19 of the 22 ran firmware susceptible to a Modbus TCP buffer overflow in MicroLogix 1400 Series B/C that Rockwell patched in 2017. The exposed population is dominated by MicroLogix 1400 — about half the total — followed by CompactLogix 1769, MicroLogix 1100 and ControlLogix 5590. The finding that should change procurement conversations: roughly 70% of the US devices reach the internet through large mobile-carrier networks, meaning cellular routers at pump stations, lift stations and unstaffed field sites. Total exposure is down 47% from a 2020 peak, and Forescout characterises the observed attacks as opportunistic exploitation at scale rather than a sophisticated targeted operation — which is the uncomfortable part, because it means the barrier to disrupting a US water utility is currently very low. - Forescout Research — Vedere Labs analysis — via Forescout, The Hacker News and CyberScoop - Scan performed 3 Aug 2026; research published 6 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter — and not one attacker needed to touch a control system
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents against industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12% on the first quarter, with manufacturing absorbing 747 of them, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The headline finding for OT teams is what did not happen: Dragos observed no case in the quarter where a ransomware operator reached Stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain or directly manipulated a control system. Where operations stopped, it followed encryption of — or precautionary shutdown because of — the enterprise IT, ERP and virtualisation layers that production depends on. Tradecraft stayed consistent: exploitation of internet-facing edge devices and remote-management tooling, abuse of valid accounts, credential theft, and EDR-killer plus bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver techniques ahead of impact. Extortion continues drifting from encryption toward data theft, so exposure persists after restoration. Dragos now tracks 119 ransomware groups touching industrial targets, up from 80 in 2024. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Dragos and Help Net Security - Report covers Q2 2026; published and reported 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway — the Node-RED interface takes commands from anyone who can reach it
item.description: Siemens’ August Patch Tuesday set, published 12 August and picked up in the CISA batch the following day, carries a maximum-severity entry: CVE-2026-58115, CVSS 10.0, in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced. The device ships a Node-RED HTTP interface that does not enforce authentication, and Node-RED’s programming nodes can run system commands. So an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the interface can author a flow and execute code on the device with maximum privileges — no credential, no exploit chain, just the product working as configured. Siemens has published fixed firmware and points operators to the Node-RED hardening guidance. The IoT2050 is used across chemical, critical manufacturing, energy and transportation, and it earns its place on this list because of where it sits: these gateways are deployed precisely to bridge process data out of the plant, which means one of their interfaces usually faces the business network. The same Siemens set also fixed a critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video Management Servers; Schneider Electric issued advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown. No public exploitation of CVE-2026-58115 has been reported. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories and CISA ICS advisory batch — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ten flaws, CVSS 9.8, no login required and no patch coming — the Ebyte gateway advisory is a replacement decision
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-237-06 on 25 August covering ten vulnerabilities in the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, firmware FW-9167-0-11. The web management interface does not enforce authentication on administrative functions (CVE-2026-73125, CVSS 9.8), relies on client-side authentication logic an unauthenticated user can simply reproduce to mint valid requests (CVE-2026-71187, CVSS 9.8), and sends MQTT credentials and control traffic in cleartext (CVE-2026-69658, CVSS 9.8). The remainder cover cleartext web transport, unprotected session tokens, cross-site request forgery, clickjacking, missing server-side authorisation and no login rate limiting. The practical impact is complete unauthorised administrative access, configuration modification, session hijack and loss of device availability. The part that changes your response: CISA records that Ebyte acknowledged the reports and said a patch was under development, then stopped responding. There is no confirmed fix, so this is a mitigate-by-isolation and plan-for-replacement item, not something to add to the patch queue. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-237-06, reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA and republished advisory text - Published 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026 — no vendor patch announced

item.title: [Critical] Two NetScaler flaws in a fortnight, one already exploited — the box most plants remote in through
item.category: Remote access — Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway
item.description: Citrix NetScaler has had a bad August, and it matters to OT because NetScaler Gateway is how a great many engineers, integrators and vendors reach plant networks. CVE-2026-8452 is a pre-authentication memory overflow in the handling of SAML authentication messages on Gateway and AAA virtual servers; watchTowr published proof-of-concept code demonstrating unauthenticated remote code execution on 14 August, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security confirmed exploitation in the wild on 17 August. Citrix scores it CVSS v4 8.8; NVD lists CVSS v3.1 9.8. Then on 19 August Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-19490, a critical authentication bypass in NetScaler ADC and Gateway at CVSS v4 9.3, remotely reachable by an unauthenticated attacker with no user interaction. No in-the-wild exploitation of the second flaw has been confirmed yet, but the pattern this year has been days, not months, between disclosure and use. - Citrix security bulletins and CCCS — reported by The Hacker News, Rapid7 and SecurityWeek - PoC 14 Aug 2026; exploitation confirmed 17 Aug 2026; CVE-2026-19490 advisory 19 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA flags an exploited Windows IKE flaw — pre-authentication SYSTEM on the box terminating your site-to-site VPN
item.category: Advisory — VPN endpoints in CISA KEV
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-33824 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: a double-free in the Microsoft Internet Key Exchange Service Extensions, rated CVSS 9.8. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send crafted IKE traffic to UDP 500 or 4500 and execute code as SYSTEM on any Windows host acting as an IPsec or IKEv2 VPN endpoint — a description that fits a great many OT jump hosts, site-to-site VPN terminators and DMZ servers. Microsoft patched it in the April 2026 update cycle, so confirmed exploitation is landing on hosts roughly four months behind, and reporting attributes the observed activity to a Chinese-speaking actor sending reverse-shell callbacks to IKE endpoints. The same KEV batch carried a VMware vCenter path traversal at CVSS 9.8, tied to a suspected China-nexus group deploying a backdoor, which matters for the virtualised SCADA, historian and HMI stacks now common in plants. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and Microsoft security updates — via CISA and The Hacker News - Added to CISA KEV 18 Aug 2026; vendor patch issued April 2026; press analysis 19 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A hard-coded key in Johnson Controls Airwall — the product many sites use to protect everything else
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-03, published 13 August, covers two flaws in Johnson Controls Airwall versions 4.0.4 and earlier: a hard-coded password and cryptographic key (CVE-2026-64887, CVSS v3 6.8) and an arbitrary file read where user-supplied input reaches filesystem access functions without adequate validation (CVE-2026-34492, CVSS v3 6.4). Chained, they allow an attacker to decrypt sensitive data, bypass authentication controls, read arbitrary files from the server and reach protected system resources. The individual scores understate the operational significance, which is what Airwall is for: it is the secure remote-access and micro-segmentation layer deployed at energy and industrial sites specifically to control who can reach what. Compromising the enforcement point undermines every asset behind it, including devices that were only ever considered acceptable because Airwall was in front of them. Johnson Controls has released version 4.1.0 and recommends applying it to all Airwalls. No public exploitation has been reported. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-03, republishing the Johnson Controls advisory — via CISA - Published 13 Aug 2026 in CISA’s 15-advisory batch; re-verified 26 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] Draft US legislation would give the EPA authority to assess water utilities and require fixes
item.description: The Water Cyber Shield Act was introduced in the US Senate on 13 August, directly in response to the coordinated attacks on more than 30 Minnesota community water systems and utilities in other states. The bill would amend the Safe Drinking Water Act and the Clean Water Act to give the EPA explicit authority to conduct cybersecurity assessments at water and wastewater systems and to require corrective action where significant vulnerabilities are found. The EPA would develop tiered cybersecurity standards in consultation with CISA, NIST, states and sector stakeholders — tiered by system size and risk rather than a single flat requirement. It authorises an additional $300 million annually through the Drinking Water and Clean Water State Revolving Funds earmarked for cybersecurity improvements, and extends federal incident-reporting obligations to state- and locally-owned systems previously outside scope. Nothing here is binding: the bill is at introduction stage and may change substantially or go nowhere. The direction of travel, however, is now unambiguous. - US Senate bill text and sponsor summary — reported via Wastewater Digest - Bill text released 10 Aug 2026; introduced and reported 13 Aug 2026; re-verified 26 Aug 2026 — not enacted

item.title: [Info] A Senate bill would put post-quantum migration on the grid’s regulatory agenda
item.description: Senators Chris Coons and Mike Rounds introduced the bipartisan Quantum-GUARD Act — the Quantum Grid Utility Assurance and Resilient Defense Act of 2026 — on 18 August. It would direct FERC to take quantum-enabled cryptographic risk into account, stand up a Department of Energy test environment for post-quantum cryptography adoption, and commission a study of quantum-related vulnerabilities across the bulk electric power system, with explicit attention to migrating both IT and operational technology. The premise is the “harvest now, decrypt later” problem: NIST finalised its first post-quantum standards in 2024, and long-lived grid assets will still be in service when those standards matter. It is an introduced bill, not law, and the OT half is the hard half — protective relays, RTUs and control-centre links have replacement cycles measured in decades, and many cannot be re-keyed in the field at all. - Senate sponsor release — reported by CyberScoop, Industrial Cyber and SC Media - Introduced 18 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The OT vendor coalition is asking CISA for a binding directive on federal building and utility control systems
item.description: The Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition, whose members are the OT security vendors most operators buy from, has pressed Congress and CISA for concrete action following the multi-state water campaign, and the asks are specific rather than rhetorical. First, a Binding Operational Directive requiring federal civilian agencies to mitigate risk in the control systems they already own — the heating and cooling, power, and access-management systems at thousands of federal sites, which are OT by any definition and are almost never treated as such. Second, reauthorisation and funding of the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program, on the grounds that small municipal utilities cannot fund this from rates. Third, extension of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act. Executive director Tatyana Bolton framed the water attacks as a wake-up call. Nothing has been issued; this is advocacy, and it signals where mandates are likely to land next. - OT Cyber Coalition statement — reported by Cybersecurity Dive, Nextgov/FCW and Government Technology - Statement late Jul 2026; coverage through 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The NSA is putting an ISA/IEC 62443 certificate in front of the controllers it buys — and the pattern will not stay inside government
item.description: ISA announced on 20 August that ISASecure is working with the US National Security Agency on a new High Criticality Component Security Assurance (HCSA) certification scheme for commercial OT components bought for National Security Systems. HCSA is derived from the existing Component Security Assurance scheme, which tests conformance to ISA/IEC 62443-4-2 component security levels, and layers on six additional technical requirements the NSA’s Operational Technology Assurance Partnership published in its 2025 report on smart controller security. Once the scheme is accepted, an HCSA certificate becomes evidence supporting a product’s inclusion on the NSA’s NSS OT Product Compliant List — in practice, a gate a smart controller passes through before it can be installed. Nothing here obliges a commercial operator. The reason it matters anyway is precedent: a government buyer with real leverage has chosen an existing 62443 conformance scheme rather than writing its own, and vendors who build to HCSA will sell those same product lines everywhere else. - ISA / ISASecure press release — corroborated by Automation World and Industrial Cyber - Announced 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026
